articles.content:
Hwang Dong-hyuk, the Emmy-winning creator and director of Netflix 's global phenomenon " Squid Game ," said he plans to "someday" return to the story that launched him into international stardom. As it stands, "Squid Game" officially ended with Season 3 in 2025, with Hwang himself confirming the end of the series. Netflix has already launched a spin-off, "Squid Game: The Challenge," with the rumor mill swirling around other possible expansions, including a U.S. remake. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Production Design — Could Something as Innovative and Cool as 'Backrooms' Find Love? Oscar Predictions: Best Adapted Screenplay — Epics, Trilogies and a Wild Dinner Party Could Define the Race

Speaking on a panel at the Doha Industry Days , the industry program of the Doha Film Festival , Hwang was asked what would be next in the world of "Squid Game." "Unfortunately, it's not mine. I don't own 'Squid Game.' Netflix owns the IP, so it's not my decision how to expand," he said.

"As far as I'm concerned, someday I'll get back to 'Squid Game,'" he added. "When I have a great idea, I'll make another one."

For now, Hwang is focused on his next feature film, "K.O. Club." The project will reunite the director with "Squid Game" star Lee Byung-hun, joined in the cast by fellow franchise alum Park Hae-soo, Oh Jung-se ("It's Okay to Not Be Okay"), Cho Yeo-jeong ("Parasite") and Kim So-jin ("The Man Standing Next"). Firstman Studio, the production company Hwang runs with producer Kim Ji-yeon, who also goes by Jenny Kim, confirmed the casting, with filming targeted for the first half of 2027.

"K.O. Club" is a dystopian sci-fi set around 20 years in the future, where the rich can buy youth. In that scenario, an increasingly desolate and disgruntled young generation starts the titular "Killing Old Men Club" to organize assassinations of the wealthy and powerful over 80. "I believe the world is getting worse and worse," Hwang said of the inspiration behind the project. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"People live longer because of technology and science, so they are not dying," he added. "Maybe they'll [get to] live to 150 years old. The rich never go away. They grab the power and money in their hands, which means the younger generation has nothing to do; they have no power, no money, no jobs."

Hwang said the effect on young people is already visible, pointing to "all those riots in Paris and everywhere."

Hwang and Kim spoke at length about the surreal experience of seeing their series blow up into one of Netflix's most-watched shows ever, a global sensation that defined culture in the pandemic years. "After the big reaction from the global audience and the success that followed, as a producer, I faced a new challenge and environment," said Kim. "Most of the people, all the people except for the main character, died during the game [in the first season], so the biggest challenge was to develop the new story with new people."

"There was pressure from Netflix," Kim or Hwang said of Season 2, which arrived three years after Season 1. "We needed to deliver it fast, and the global audience was waiting for the next season. We were always getting questions: 'Where is Season 2? Season 3?' It was a nightmare."

The team kept the production process the same across seasons, Kim said, largely to meet the expectations of "Squid Game" fans all over the world. "What was it that fans liked about 'Squid Game'? We tried to maintain that."

Hwang said he never tries to "make something that people like." "I always try to make what I like to make while at the same time hoping and praying people like what I like to make. If I lose that mindset, I'll go crazy."

"When I first wrote the script, the beginning point of my creative process was when I was poor," he recalled. "I didn't have much money and imagined: What if it was me? Would I enter this kind of competition and try to win the prize? I was so broke in 2009. I was so broke. I only had like $5 in my account."

Hwang recalled reading Japanese comics and manga about survival games where the tasks were "mentally, intellectually, and physically difficult." "A guy like me could not survive [it]. I started thinking like that. What if there was something where a normal guy like me could not only compete but become a winner? That's how I developed the idea of 'Squid Game.'" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Because Season 1 was so well received by a global audience, Hwang said, he had the self-belief that Seasons 2 and 3 would also be loved. "I tried to brainwash myself throughout the creative process."

"I felt more free to do things my own way," he added. "I believe that the success of the first series, whatever the previous success was, was leverage, an asset, to be able to take bigger risks. When you have big success, everybody believes you. No matter what you say, they say I love it. That's when you take a big risk in your life. That's the only chance."

As for what's next for Firstman Studio, Kim said the company's credibility went up after "Squid Game," but that it remains a very small company. "We're not making a lot of projects. The reason we want to do this is that, as an independent producer, rather than focusing on profitability, we want to focus on taking the right creative risks to create what we believe in."

articles.title: 'White Tiger Column' Review: Young Resistance Fighters in Myanmar Are Trained for War, but Not Yet for Life, in a Delicate Doc Study
articles.summary: A nasal R&B jam by Justin Bieber isn't everyone's idea of comfort listening, least of all played on a crackly phone speaker. But when the singer's 2020 hit "Intentions" plays midway through "White Tiger Column," briefly bonding two teen female soldiers in a moment of bubbly release and actual acting-their-age joy, it's like a shot […]
articles.content:
A nasal R&B jam by Justin Bieber isn't everyone's idea of comfort listening, least of all played on a crackly phone speaker. But when the singer's 2020 hit "Intentions" plays midway through " White Tiger Column ," briefly bonding two teen female soldiers in a moment of bubbly release and actual acting-their-age joy, it's like a shot of oxygen to Robert Mentov , Dwight Jantzi and Bryan Dickie 's subtly upsetting documentary. Later on, Taylor Swift's "You Belong With Me" likewise sticks out like a sweet, sore thumb in the film's otherwise severe milieu: a remote Burmese jungle camp where GenZ volunteer recruits in the Myanmar People's Defense Force are put through their paces, in the hope of standing up to the country's military junta. It's an unduly weighty calling at such a tender age; youth must occasionally, giddily assert itself. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Film Editing — ‘You Can See Everything’ Looks to Crash a Race of Past Winners and Become the Third Documentary Ever Nominated Steven Spielberg Calls ‘The Odyssey’ a ‘Showstopper’ and ‘One of the Greatest Things’ Matt Damon Has Ever Done

The opening film of this year's IDFA documentary festival, "White Tiger Column" takes on a large, raw subject: the fostering of a resistance movement and mentality, from the ground up, in the wake of the 2021 coup that saw Myanmar's new, democratically elected government overthrown by the country's army. But it does so with delicate humanity, its focus less on collective rhetoric and conflict than on the many individual fragilities and growing pains within an improvised, makeshift corps. Spanning six weeks of basic training, the film doesn't limn a neat coming-of-age arc: Nobody enters the camp a boy and leaves a man, but this underdog army works with the inexperienced rebels they have.

A directorial collaboration between Dickie — a Canadian photographer specializing in sites of sociopolitical upheaval — and compatriots Jantzi and Mentov, founders of the hitherto more fiction-oriented Nocte Films studio, "White Tiger Column" takes an approach between the journalistic and the more ambiently observational. There are no talking-head interviews or information beyond some scene-setting title cards, but a patient sense of human interest prevails, as the filmmakers embed themselves in the camp for a full course of training, observing its process without interference. The human subjects are not named, but personalities and personal crises emerge from a rigid, would-be military routine. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In some senses, "White Tiger Column" follows a structure familiar from many a basic-training drama, as unformed young people reckon with the new strictures and challenges of army life. But the stakes here are very different, not least because everyone present is there by dint of their own urgent belief — having fled to the jungle to escape the reach of the country's actual military overlords. "To fight the government, we must become soldiers ourselves," they are reminded by their commanders, who have little more authority or experience than the recruits they're leading. And the goal here is not mere national service or self-improvement: "I don't want to just train, I want to fight," says one newcomer, speaking for many of his peers who can't wait to get their hands on a weapon.

In other respects, however, they're just kids, and their vulnerability and naïveté are all the more exposed by these extreme circumstances. "I miss my bed, my fridge, my TV, my mom and dad," says one, sounding less like a soldier than a homesick child at a summer camp — which the boot camp quite frequently resembles, with its tranquil setting, team-building, fireside bonding and weekly calls home. Less so the lessons in homemade explosives and rite-of-passage tattooing: adult reminders of the grim responsibilities and dangers that await them after a too-brief education in the ways of war. Upon completing their training, an instructor tells them: "From now on, we are comrades, though you may call me teacher if you wish." In the resistance, ultimately, everyone's just figuring it out.

It's tough-minded but not without stray moments of tenderness and joy — particularly when focused on the friendship between two intrepid female recruits, a conspicuous minority in the collective — or of lush cinematic beauty, as Mentov, also the film's accomplished DP, can hardly fail to capture the verdant, shadow-streaked riches of the environment around them. But the filmmakers aren't inclined to romanticize matters, either in terms of character-based narratives or ideological emphasis: In this simultaneously stirring and frightening portrait, we know exactly what everyone's fighting for, but as one near-child soldier admits, "we only have theories about what might happen."

articles.title: We All Love Batman but These 5 Things Annoy Even the Most Diehard Fans
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics Let's be real for second: it's a Batman world and we're all just living in it. The Caped Crusader first premiered in 1939's Detective Comics #27 and quickly became one of the most popular of the new breed of adventure heroes. Superman was something new and that's why he became so popular so fast, but […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Let's be real for second: it's a Batman world and we're all just living in it. The Caped Crusader first premiered in 1939's Detective Comics #27 and quickly became one of the most popular of the new breed of adventure heroes. Superman was something new and that's why he became so popular so fast, but Batman was more like already known characters like the Spirit or the Phantom. Once Robin showed up in the 1940, it was all gas, no brakes and soon the Dark Knight was at the top of the superhero community, a place where he's stayed ever since. He's the most popular superhero of them all, and in a lot of ways, nearly everyone is a fan of Batman.

If you like DC Comics, you usually have to have at least a little esteem for the character, because you're going to be seeing him a lot. This has become a problem over the years for a lot of fans, though, because Bats can get a tad annoying at times. He's inescapable and even for fans of the heroes, it can be exasperating. Batman is one of the best fictional characters ever created, but even his biggest fans are annoyed with these five things.

Comics are all about passion. You don't become a comic creator if you don't love the medium and you don't work on superheroes unless you're devoted to them on another level. Creators enter the industry with a list of characters they want to do and Batman is always on the list. Whenever a writer or artist hits a certain level of fame, DC comes a-calling, and there's always one character they bring with them – Batman. Look at every A-lister who has joined DC in the last few years and you'll see a lot of them starting out on Batman books.

Everyone wants to do Batman , so everyone says yes, but it might have been better if (just using this as an example) Jason Aaron got to start his latest run at DC with another character, maybe one that isn't seen as much but he liked more. Every creator has that one low-level character they have a story for (I'm not even a comic writer – yet – and I have one; ask me about my Hourman pitch, DC) but instead of starting there, they all start on Batman. Batman doesn't need every A-list talent and as we've seen in the past, when you put great talent on even Z-list characters, you get something special. However, we have to feed the Bat-God the talent of our best creators at all times to keep it satiated.

DC made the multiverse popular in comics in the 1960s, beginning a process of introducing numerous versions of readers' favorite heroes and villains. Back then, most of the dupes we got were just other heroic versions; the closest we got to evil multiversal versions of heroes are the characters of Earth-Three and they even had different names (which I think has more to do with not confusing the young readers than anything else – it seems like something Julie Schwartz would have made an editorial mandate back then). However, as the industry changed and grim and gritty comics became the order of the day, we started to get darker alternate Earths, which led to the many evil versions of heroes.

Every popular hero has had at least one memorable villainous multiversal dupe, but because it's Batman he has more of them. Some of them only appear in one story and some, like Owlman or the Batman Who Laughs, show up all the time. Evil Batmen usually aren't even all that interesting – they're just the same Batman we always get, except they've decided to kill. While sometimes, evil dupes can be intriguing, Batman's usually aren't and they're always on the verge of introducing a new one.

Batman and the Joker are locked in a death spiral and it's one we've been watching with rapt attention for decades. There are few grudges more serious than theirs and some of the best DC stories of all-time have the two of them going at it (and we're not talking fanfic going at it). Everybody wants to write their Batman vs the Joker story and that's where we come to the problem. Everyone has a Batman story and everyone has a Joker story, and since both characters sell, we get those stories.

Batman has some of the best villains ever and everyone wants to work with them, however, this also means that we're stuck with the same villains. It's made worse by "writing for the trade". This means that we get a minimum of four months worth of issues with one villain as the focus, with smaller villains dropping to the wayside. The big villains suck all of the oxygen out of the room and we never get to see the lower-level yet still cool villains, like Firebug or Killer Moth or Kite-Man. You can't move a villain up on the food chain of popularity if they don't appear.

Comics are a great medium for storytelling, but they are also a business. You have to pay people to make these stories and publish them, so you have to make money. Batman is one of the most successful fictional characters of all-time. His books sell very well, to the extent that DC publishes more Batman books per month than anything else. If you're a fan of Batman, there's no way you aren't eating well because as we talked about back in entry 5, every A-lister has a Batman story and DC is going to publish it.

There are so many Batman stories every month, it's not funny. Having a lot of choices can be a great thing, but it gets to the point when there's just too much. We don't need yet another out of continuity, 12-issue Batman story by an A-list team of creators. There have been times in the not-so distant past (2021) when DC mostly published Batman. It's annoying to the extreme, but until the Dark Knight stops selling, we're never going to see an end to his stories.

Online comic spaces can be described as the Thunderdome. Sure, a lot of people agree on a lot of things, but arguing is the name of the game and everyone likes to play "who would win". Eventually, everyone brings up Batman fighting some ridiculously powerful hero or villain and utters two of the most dreaded words in online comics discourse – "prep time". And look, we've all done it when we got frustrated with the arguments, dropping prep time like a Tsar Bomba on your opponents. That doesn't make it any less annoying.

Batman whips powerful heroes all the time and prep time is key to all of them. What makes it so annoying is that it's always plausible. Bruce Wayne is a billionaire genius with access to technology that is basically magic. Batman can figure out a way to beat, let's say, Lucifer with enough prep time. He can do that to anyone. It's one of the most annoying parts of reading Batman comics and the most annoying part about arguing about Batman.

What about Batman annoys you the most? What would you change about the character to fix that? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.content:
The International Film Festival Rotterdam ( IFFR ) has unveiled the first works in its immersive strands, inviting audiences "into strange worlds where our choices have unexpected consequences."

IFFR recently revealed a first wave of world premieres for its 56th edition, taking place Jan. 28- Feb. 7. On Thursday, it revealed first offerings in its Art Directions, Lightroom and Sound//vision programs.

Art Directions focuses on "installations, expanded cinema, performance, XR and sound, exploring different ways audiences can encounter and inhabit moving-image work." This year's program includes its first-ever Artist in Focus, namely the Catalan collective Servicios Inmersivos. Meanwhile, IFFR’s Lightroom initiatives support immersive and interactive practices at different stages. "Art Directions has always been a space where we can challenge our understanding of what cinema can be," said Melissa van der Schoor, chief of content at IFFR. "This year’s selection takes us beneath the streets of New York, explores the relationship between belief and everyday life, and invites us into strange worlds where our choices have unexpected consequences. What excites me is how these artists use such different approaches to make us question what we see, what we take for granted and how we experience the world around us." articles.title: My Assistant Scammed Me. Then Did Far Worse to Demi Moore.
articles.summary: Years after stealing from me, an identity thief went after the star. Now out of prison, she says she’s a brand new person.
articles.content:
In March of 2018, someone walked into a FedEx office in Beverly Hills to pick up a package addressed to Demi Moore .

This person wasn't Moore's assistant, though the badge said otherwise. He had never met the actress and had no legitimate reason to be collecting her mail. But he knew the tracking number, the original shipping address and exactly what was inside the package: Moore's American Express Black Card.

Over the next three weeks, he'd charge nearly $170,000 to the card while Moore was in Idaho, unaware of what was happening back in Los Angeles. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Lifestyle Baby2Baby Gala Fetes Demi Moore and Raises Over $20M for the Cause TV 'Landman' Ups 4 Actors to Series Regulars as Season 3 Begins Filming

And the person who walked out of that FedEx office with her card was someone I knew.

David Matthew Read wasn't what you would picture when you hear "mastermind criminal." Blond-haired and blue-eyed with a dimple poking out of one cheek, he was disarmingly forthcoming, sweet and funny. We first met in 2011, when he was in his late 20s and I was in my early 40s. I needed help hanging curtains, and a friend introduced me to him as a friend from church. Soon, David was somewhere between my part-time assistant and bestie, helping me with everything from errands to booking travel to prepping for parties.

It was only once I'd given him access to everything — including my P.O. Box, where he picked up my mail for me — that the friend who'd introduced us told me that David had actually been in prison a few years earlier for committing bank fraud.

But, the friend assured me, David was so trustworthy now that the church let him use their credit card to buy décor for their office. And when I asked David about the fraud and prison sentence, he was so forthcoming, so lacking in excuses and so willing to admit he'd done something wrong that I immediately pushed his crime out of my head. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Still, a few months into our arrangement, I realized that as an underemployed freelance writer, I didn't actually need an assistant. Also, something about David had begun to seem off; he'd claim to be able to do things he couldn't, and I'd only realize this when he'd present the "finished" result — a website, an Ikea bookshelf, research — and it was so unfinished that I wouldn't know what to even say.

When I let him know that I no longer had work for him, he was sweet and understanding; he drove off in his orange convertible Mitsubishi Eclipse, and I figured that was the end of that.

And it was — until a few months later, when I got a call from Citibank that I owed nearly $7,000 on a credit card bill. Positive that it was a mistake, I had the representative read off the card number.

"It's not mine," I responded, relieved.

Oh, but it was, she explained. It was an additional card on my account, issued in the name of David Read.

As she read off the list of charges, I fell into a shame spiral. How could I have been stupid enough to give a convicted criminal so much access to my life?

I don‘t remember exactly what David said when I first confronted him, just that he initially denied everything and then rather quickly confessed. He told me he'd only done it because the church needed him to buy certain things and, as a convicted felon, he couldn't get a credit card, and so he'd intercepted my credit card bill one day when picking up my mail and ordered a card in his name under my account. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

When I read out charges we both knew couldn't have been made for even the loosest of churches — to, among other places, Good Microbrew, The Abbey, Mickey's, Hooters, Malibu Family Wines, DMH Aesthetics and a dating website called Successful Match — he admitted that his motivation had nothing to do with the church. He'd just wanted a credit card and didn't have another way to get one.

David didn't cry or plead for forgiveness. He calmly explained that he'd never wanted me to be financially responsible, which is why he'd been paying the charges for months; he just needed some time to get some money together. In the end, the friend who'd introduced us paid off the credit card and told David to pay him back by making regular donations to their church. (David ended up leaving the church shortly after.)

And so David became a part of my past, the I-got-scammed-by-an-assistant story I eventually forgot about.

Until July of 2018, when the friend who'd introduced us sent me a link to an OK! magazine story that David had done something similar to Demi Moore.

A few months ago, mainly out of curiosity, I decided to see if I could find David. It took roughly four minutes: I logged onto a public records website, plopped in his name and emailed the four potential email addresses it provided: Are you the David Read that once worked for me?

A few minutes later, "Hi Anna please give me a call," with a phone number appeared in my inbox. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

A few minutes after that, my cell buzzed with a text: "Is this Anna you just emailed me."

I was surprised by how easy it had been to track down a guy who'd spent 55 months in prison. But I was even more surprised by the name and photo that popped up on my iPhone alongside the text.

David Read was now Taylor Read Madison. The person I'd known as a man was now living as a woman.

Three days later, I sat across from Taylor at Liberation Café in Hollywood, splitting a breakfast burrito, Alanis Morissette playing in the background. The blond hair, blue eyes and dimple remained, but the hair was now long and tucked into a ponytail, the nails were painted, the dimple was decorated with a dash of blush and she was wearing a smattering of jewelry — including a diamond wedding ring.

Taylor felt both familiar and unfamiliar. As I watched her whip a hook out of her white purse and latch it onto the table before daintily placing the purse on it to keep it from sitting on the ground, I couldn't help but notice that she seemed nervous.

And, of course, she had every reason to be. She also had every reason to not want to make her story public. So why was she here?

To tell this story, it helps to go back to the beginning.

Pennington Gap, Virginia, is the kind of place where you might expect a woman to receive a hefty settlement when her husband died of black lung.

And that was indeed what happened to Caroline Rhea, Taylor's maternal grandmother. Because of the settlement and the fact that she was "good with credit cards" (a fact Taylor tells me without a hint of irony), Caroline could shower the grandchild she raised with clothing that she might not have otherwise been able to afford. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"My grandmother was a little bit over-caring," Taylor says now. "I think she felt guilty that my mother wasn't able to raise me, and so she overcompensated." (Taylor Read Madison has given me permission to use her former name and pronouns when describing events that occurred before her transition.)

From an early age, David learned that "stuff" could make up for things like having a mother who couldn't take care of you and a father who wasn't around. Even though David and his grandmother lived in a single-wide trailer, "people thought I lived a completely different life," Taylor explains. He helped perpetuate the delusion by getting off the bus early so the other kids didn't see where he lived.

The fraud started innocently enough. When David was 19 and attending Mountain Empire Community College in Big Stone Gap, Virginia, he began dating a 50-something attorney named Sam (not his real name) and quickly moved into Sam's three-story, six-bedroom house. After about a year, their relationship had cooled, and Sam actually moved a new boyfriend in. But the house was so chaotic and unstructured that instead of moving out, David just relocated to a different bedroom.

The chaos extended to Sam's financial life. "Sam was terrible with money," Taylor says. "He was paying off his credit cards with credit cards, just living well beyond his means. And he had me on all his cards."

One day, it occurred to David that Sam probably wouldn't even notice if David bought himself a car. And that's how he ended up driving a 1995 Oldsmobile Aurora out to L.A., his pockets filled with roughly $6,000 that he'd accumulated slowly by making periodic ATM withdrawals from Sam's account. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

David came to L.A. ostensibly to meet a guy he'd been talking to online, but when he arrived and learned that the guy still lived with his ex-boyfriend, he didn't care. He'd made it to L.A., the shiny place he'd always wanted to come to — a place where you could entirely reinvent yourself so long as you dressed the part.

"Why do you think God invented credit? For fabulous people like me." Demi Moore (Jules) in St. Elmo's Fire

Scamming Demi Moore was never part of the plan. It probably wouldn't have ever happened if David hadn't been doing a lot of meth and hanging out with a druggy crowd.

It all started when David met a guy named Ray in December 2017, and Ray told him that he had access to an account someone who'd worked at Federal Express had sold him. Ray explained the scheme: American Express sends all its cards via FedEx, and with access to the FedEx back end, you could log in and route the card to any location you wanted.

David had inadvertently stumbled upon the ideal project for a meth-using, tech-savvy guy with a history of credit card fraud: He got access to the account from Ray, downloaded what he found in the FedEx system and started cross-referencing names and addresses of cardholders using Google's My Maps feature. Eventually, he was able to connect tracking numbers to people's names, phone numbers, business names and addresses. (FedEx did not respond to repeated requests for comment.)

At first, he didn't know why some names were marked "titanium." Then he realized it was code for the coveted Black Card — also known as the Centurion card — an invitation-only program that allegedly requires a minimum annual spend of $500,000 and is said to include everything from private jet arrangements and exclusive restaurant reservations to VIP treatment at luxury hotels. "I freaked out a little," Taylor recalls. "I remember thinking, 'What can I get with this? Everything.' " blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

When David saw Demi Moore's name on the spreadsheet with the word titanium next to it, he didn't care about who it was. He just had an idea of how he could get his hands on her card. "Demi Moore wasn't a target," Taylor says. "She was a convenience."

In the back end of the FedEx database, David redirected her card from her business manager at Nigro Karlin Segal Feldstein & Bolno in Century City to a FedEx store in Beverly Hills.

"At the time, all you needed to pick up a card was the tracking number, the name it was going to and the original shipping address," Taylor says. For added insurance, David made himself a badge that said he was an assistant at Moore's holding company, Pajama Party Productions. Once he knew the card had been sent, he parked his (fraudulently purchased) Mercedes E-Class in front of the FedEx store, walked in with his badge and announced he was there to pick up a package for Moore. The clerk handed it over.

Then David drove to a Century City parking lot and called a friend who had access to a black-market website. Within a few minutes (after sending the friend $8 through his Cash App), David had Moore's Social Security number.
